skill.name: Comma between a dependent and a main clause
skill.why: The comma shows readers where the 'if' part stops and the main part starts.
skill.how: Starts with when, if, because or although? Put a comma where that part ends.

steps.say: This part has a doer and an action. Say it aloud.
steps.ask: Does it make sense on its own?

check.nudge: Say it again. When the bell rang... then what happened? Do you know?

steps.win: Right! It waits. When is a joining word, or conjunction.

steps.say: A doer plus an action is a clause. This has three.

show.nudge: When the bell rang... then what? It leaves you waiting. Try another part.
Because it was snowing... what happened? It leaves you waiting.

steps.ask: Tap the part that makes sense on its own.
steps.win: Yes! Main clause, or independent clause. The others are dependent.

steps.say: A dependent clause at the start needs a comma after.

show.nudge: When Zed... did what? The when part isn't finished yet.
That comma would split the game from what it did. Where does the when part end?

steps.ask: Tap the word the comma goes after.
steps.win: Yes! The comma goes where the dependent clause ends.

steps.say: No comma, and the crew eats the yeti!

show.nudge: While the crew... did what? The while part isn't finished yet.
Now the crew ate the yeti! Where does the while part really end?

steps.ask: Tap the word the comma goes after, so the yeti is safe.

steps.say: Long one! The comma goes just before the main clause.

show.nudge: The snowflake belongs to the 'as soon as' part. Who does the main thing?
Fell is an action, not a doer. Who did something in the main clause?

steps.ask: Tap the doer of the main clause.
steps.win: Yes! The penguins start the main clause. Comma after fell.

steps.say: Gus always adds a comma. Here, the main clause comes first.

options.text: We ran outside when the bell rang.
We ran outside, when the bell rang.
options.reason: The main clause comes first here, so nothing is hanging on at the start. Does it need a comma?

options.text: We ran outside. When the bell rang.
options.reason: Say 'When the bell rang.' alone. It leaves you waiting, so it can't be a sentence.

steps.win: Yes! Main clause first? No comma needed.

terms.means: A clause that starts with a word like when, because or if. It can't stand alone.
A clause that makes sense on its own. Every sentence needs one.
And and but join two whole thoughts. When, because, although make one part need the other.

card.test: Dependent clause first? Comma where it ends. Main clause first? No comma.

weDo.hint: Find the part that can't stand alone. Where does it end?
weDo.success: 'When the snow stopped' can't stand alone. The comma goes where it ends, before 'we'.

options.text: When the snow stopped, we built a fort.
When the snow stopped we, built a fort.
options.reason: The comma splits 'we' from what we did. Where does the 'when' part finish?

options.text: When the snow stopped. We built a fort.
options.reason: 'When the snow stopped.' can't stand alone, so it can't be a sentence.

weDo.prompt: Which version is punctuated so the penguin is safe?
weDo.hint: Read each one aloud. Is anyone cooking the penguin?
weDo.success: The comma after 'cooking' ends the dependent clause. Mo cooks, and the penguin just dances.

options.text: While Mo was cooking, the penguin danced.
While Mo was cooking the penguin danced.
options.reason: With no comma, it first reads as if Mo was cooking the penguin!

options.text: While Mo was cooking the penguin, danced.
options.reason: Now Mo really is cooking the penguin, and 'danced' has no doer.

encounters.frame: The orchestra program says: As soon as the conductor raised her baton, the whole orchestra fell silent.

options.text: 'Raised her baton' is the main clause, so a comma goes straight after it.
options.reason: 'Raised her baton' has no doer of its own. Which part makes sense alone?

options.text: Readers need to breathe after the baton goes up, so the pause goes there.
options.reason: Commas aren't for breathing. Which clause does this comma close?

options.text: The 'as soon as' clause ends at 'baton'. The main clause starts after it.
'As soon as the conductor' tells you when, so either spot would be fine.
options.reason: That leaves out what the conductor did. Where does the whole 'as soon as' part end?
